james-ratcliffe.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
james-ratcliffe.period: Project One support, 2023; policy advocacy and Grangemouth agreement, 2025
james-ratcliffe.summary: Ratcliffe publicly sought policy relief for industry, while INEOS secured named government-backed investments. These are concrete state–business relationships, but the reviewed record also shows public-interest conditions rather than an unrestricted personal windfall.
james-ratcliffe.mechanism: Industrial policy advocacy ↔ government-backed investment with public safeguards

support.text: Reuters reports Ratcliffe personally urging Britain to reduce environmental costs on businesses, presenting high costs as a barrier to investment.

The UK announced more than £120 million of government support within a £150 million joint Grangemouth investment. Its release quotes Ratcliffe welcoming the partnership. These are announced project amounts, not personal payments.
UK Export Finance disclosed €700 million principal support for INEOS Project One and named the participating UK exporters. It is export-finance support, not a €700 million cash gift to Ratcliffe.
support.source: UK Export Finance: supported project notice

counter.text: The Grangemouth announcement identifies jobs and critical supply chains as public objectives. It restricts funding to site improvements, requires an operational commitment, and gives government a right to share future profits.
UKEF required environmental and social performance monitoring. Its notice describes an export-support decision subject to standards, not a finding of political favoritism.

james-ratcliffe.limitations: The estimate concerns documented industrial-policy bargaining, not corruption or a claim that lobbying caused these awards. Announced support is not audited disbursement or profit. The chemicals plant is distinct from the closed oil refinery. Broad industry relief is not exclusive personal privilege.

stephen-ross.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
stephen-ross.period: Hudson Yards reporting, 2017–2019; city elections, 2021; western-yard proposal, 2025
stephen-ross.summary: Ross combined substantial electoral spending with a development business benefiting from public financing and tax incentives. That overlap supports an influence estimate, not a claim that his donations purchased a particular approval.
stephen-ross.mechanism: Private electoral spending ↔ publicly enabled urban development

support.text: The Campaign Finance Board lists Stephen M. Ross as Common Sense NYC’s largest contributor, at $1 million. The committee spent about $1.52 million in City Council races; its total spending is not all Ross’s personal expenditure.
support.source: NYC Campaign Finance Board: 2021 post-election report, p. 93

support.text: Forbes interviews Ross about Hudson Yards and distinguishes an estimated $1.4 billion in tax breaks from $4 billion of other city investment. Those aggregate figures are not a direct payment of the entire sum to him.
support.kind: Reported business benefit and subject interview

support.text: IBO explains that qualifying commercial developments receive discounted payments in lieu of property taxes, whereas residential and hotel developments generally pay full taxes. It separately identifies city infrastructure and interest support.
support.source: NYC Independent Budget Office: Hudson Yards fiscal brief
support.access: Indexed PDF passages reviewed; direct URL now redirects

counter.text: Ross defended the development as connected to the wider city rather than an exclusive enclave. Public infrastructure can benefit others as well as the developer; the full city investment is not his private gain.

The city’s June 2025 western-yard announcement describes a tentative deal including affordable homes, public space and a school, using future project tax revenue for infrastructure. Proposed delivery is not proof of completed public benefits.

stephen-ross.limitations: Historical episode estimate, not proof of vote buying, guaranteed election outcomes or a quid pro quo. The 2021 donations postdate the earlier Hudson Yards arrangements. District-wide costs, tax concessions and company receipts are different quantities. This review does not audit later financing or assign all Related activity to Ross.

idan-ofer.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
idan-ofer.summary: Ofer personally joined high-level lobbying over ICL’s resource-tax exposure. The narrow episode shows political access and investment leverage, but the company’s own subsequent filing confirms that the contested tax legislation passed.
idan-ofer.mechanism: Prime-ministerial access and investment pressure → unsuccessful attempt to stop a tax reform

support.text: Globes reports Ofer, the controlling shareholder of Israel Corporation, meeting Netanyahu with ICL chairman Nir Gilad during the effort to remove the resource-tax recommendations from the budget bill.
support.source: Globes: Stella Korin-Lieber and Amiram Barkat

support.text: ICL’s response to the interim recommendations warned that the proposed regime would curtail investment in Israel. This documents the company’s bargaining position, not an independently verified economic forecast.
support.source: ICL: public response to interim recommendations

support.text: ICL reported that the Knesset approved legislation implementing Sheshinski II on 18 November 2015 and anticipated an adverse effect on profits, dependent on potash prices.

counter.text: The Prime Minister’s Office characterized the meeting as normal dialogue and said no decisions had been taken; the finance minister supported the reform.
The company’s enactment notice contradicts a claim that the campaign prevented the reform. It does not measure whether lobbying affected any details.

idan-ofer.limitations: The zero benefit level is confined to stopping this reform, not a finding of no concessions or political advantages anywhere in Ofer’s career. The score does not cover later Dead Sea arrangements, whose assets and compensation require separate valuation. Company conduct is attributed to him only where personal involvement is reported.

michal-strnad.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
michal-strnad.period: Slovak framework, December 2025; IPO and company disclosures, 2026
michal-strnad.summary: Strnad’s leadership and CSG’s major government procurement framework are documented. The framework’s headline value is not booked revenue, and the reviewed material does not establish his personal influence over the award or preferential terms.
michal-strnad.mechanism: Owner-led defense supplier → public procurement; individual political mechanism unresolved

support.text: The IPO announcement identifies Michal Strnad as owner and chairman, and names him for the chair/CEO role after the proposed corporate conversion.
support.access: Indexed PDF passage reviewed; direct URL redirected to a generic page

support.text: CSG’s annual results describe ZVS Holding’s seven-year Slovak Ministry of Defence framework for ammunition for Slovakia and other EU states, with a potential value up to €58 billion.

counter.text: CSG explicitly says €58 billion is a potential framework value, not a committed order book. Individual orders are required, and approximately €1 billion was included in the pipeline at the results announcement. Pipeline is not recognized revenue.

michal-strnad.limitations: No numerical estimate from defense-sector exposure or contract size alone. The company’s response is an interested-party statement, not independent validation. Personal political intervention, award comparisons and realized preferential gains need further evidence. No claim that the framework funded his IPO is adopted.

suleiman-kerimov-family.reviewDepth: Source-led episode review; not independently editorially reviewed
suleiman-kerimov-family.period: Uralkali purchase and sale discussions, 2010–2013; Treasury action, 2022
suleiman-kerimov-family.summary: Kerimov’s parliamentary position and politically sensitive investments provide substantial reasons for scrutiny. This file nevertheless separates documented office-holding from unverified claims that political protection produced particular financial benefits.
suleiman-kerimov-family.mechanism: Public office and strategic investments; extent of preferential protection unresolved

support.text: Treasury identifies Kerimov as a Federation Council member and states that his 2018 designation was for being a Russian government official. Its 2022 notice blocks a trust in which it says he retained an interest.

Combined Reuters, Bloomberg and Moscow Times reporting records his 25% Uralkali purchase and describes investor expectations that a Kremlin-loyal buyer would reduce political risk. Expectations are not a demonstrated concession awarded to him.
support.source: The Moscow Times: combined reports on Uralkali sale

counter.text: The same acquisition report cites a source saying the purchase price exceeded market value. It does not establish that Kerimov acquired the stake at a state-engineered discount.
counter.source: The Moscow Times: transaction pricing qualification

counter.text: Reuters reports the Russian government ruling out a state purchase of his stake during the 2013 Belarus dispute, while leaving open a private trade sale. That limits a claim of an assured public bailout.

suleiman-kerimov-family.limitations: No numerical position yet: public office and designation are not substitutes for evaluating every dimension. This review does not resolve the causal effect of political protection or reconstruct financing terms. Family wealth is not assigned identical conduct. Separate French tax and yacht disputes are outside this file; no criminal finding is inferred from the designation.

rationales: Direct public policy advocacy by the owner-executive.
Named corporate financing and investment support, qualified by conditions and public objectives.
Investment, policy advocacy and a negotiated public partnership overlap; a personal reciprocal bargain is not established.
A large individually attributed contribution to a city-election spending vehicle.
Specific tax incentives and public infrastructure support for the associated development, not all private proceeds.
Documented political spending and public-facing development interests coexist; chronology does not prove purchased favors.
A named personal meeting about an economically relevant policy dispute.
The objective of stopping the tax reform was not achieved: enactment is documented, rather than assumed from silence.
Political access and investment pressure are linked within the campaign, but the law’s passage limits evidence of successful feedback.
